lesson.title: Audio Distortion: Two Families of Unwanted Sound
lesson.summary: Audio distortion is the general term for any unwanted alteration a nonlinear circuit adds to a signal, and nearly all of it falls into the two families already covered: harmonic distortion from a single tone, and intermodulation distortion from multiple tones interacting.
lesson.body:
Real audio signals, the kind covered in the audio signal concept, are almost never a single pure tone the way the worked examples in the last two chapters simplified things to be. That means a real circuit processing real music or speech is generating harmonic distortion and intermodulation distortion at the same time, continuously, from the same nonlinearity: each frequency present acts somewhat like its own individual tone generating its own harmonics, while all of those frequencies simultaneously interact with each other to generate intermodulation products as well. Audio distortion, as a general term, covers both effects together, even though the two previous chapters measured them separately.

Splitting distortion into these two separate measurements is still genuinely useful, because each one isolates a different aspect of a circuit's nonlinearity for testing purposes. A THD measurement deliberately uses a single sine wave as its input, specifically so that no intermodulation can occur, isolating pure harmonic behavior. An IMD measurement deliberately uses two carefully chosen tones, specifically to isolate intermodulation behavior instead. Neither number alone fully predicts how distorted a complex piece of real music will sound, but together they characterize a circuit's nonlinear behavior from two complementary angles.

Here is a worked example connecting a distortion percentage back to an actual voltage. Suppose a preamp is specified at 1 percent THD while amplifying a 5 V RMS signal. The actual RMS voltage of the unwanted harmonic distortion energy riding along on top of the wanted signal is 0.01 times 5 V, which equals 0.05 V RMS.

As a general rule of thumb, distortion above roughly 1 percent is often noticeable on revealing program material, while distortion well under 0.1 percent is generally considered transparent on most equipment, though this is only a loose guideline, since how the distortion energy is distributed across harmonics, and how much intermodulation distortion accompanies it, matters just as much as the raw percentage figure. The single most common real world cause of a sudden, severe jump in both harmonic and intermodulation distortion together is a signal running out of voltage headroom and clipping, which is exactly where this sequence goes next.
